The additional information is evaluated in order to select a final corridor that is approximately one (1) mile in width. It is to be noted that within the corridor stage other viable modes are evaluated in order to provide the transportation facility that will meet the requirements of the area studied and to provide for the mobility of people, goods, and services.
The design stage consists of the detailed analysis of alternatives within the approximate one (1) mile final corridor. The alternative alignments within this corridor regardless of mode would be studied on the previously discussed issues. A public hearing would again be held for conveying the data evaluated and for soliciting detailed pertinent people value data in order to determine the final selection of an alternative. This alternative would have an optimum beneficial affect on the area, the people within the region, and the communities affected by the final alternative.
In the case of an existing arterial (i.e., U.S. 30, Lincoln Highway), the two stages (Corridor and Design) are combined into one stage called a Combined Corridor and Design.
A. Other Modes
The Regional Transportation Interim Plan and Program was developed based upon travel desires. Because travel desires are used in developing the transportation model, the alternate travel modes are not in competition. All modes are needed in order to build an integrated transport system.
No east-west commuter rail transit system now exists in or near the study corridor or in adjacent communities. It is extremely doubtful that the population and terminal employment densities will ever increase in these suburban fringe areas to a point justifying 'new right-of-way for construction of an east-west rail mass transit system.
In looking at the macro-mode aspects of an integrated transportation system a Northwestern University study states:
Metropolitan areas with low density of population (central city below 10,000 persons per square mile) are less likely to develop supporting revenue for rail-rapid-transit systems than are metropolitan areas with higher densities.
